catalog_quote: 2.2.3. En gogo, les oppositions ont été encore plus réduites, puisque les thèmes *-cvcv ont été intégralement ramenés à une réalisation unique, à savoir: accent sur l'antépénultième³. Exemples: – schèmes BB: dent *-gègò íjego; jambe *-gùdù múgulu – schèmes HB: huile *-kụ́tà máfuta; pluie *-bụ́dà mvûla – schèmes BH: canne à sucre *-gùbá íguva; oiseau *-dègé ndêje – schèmes HH: graine *-béyú mbêyu; poulet *-kúkú ŋkûku [fn. 3] Quand le mot est dissyllabique, l'accent antépénultième se réalise comme un ton tombant. [p. 418] En revanche, les thèmes *-cv̀v̀cv́ manifestent encore une opposition: ils sont les seuls à avoir donné, en gogo, un accent sur la pénultième (les seuls pour les nominaux, car ce schème peut être aussi observé dans certaines formes conjuguées). Exemples: – schèmes BB: bovin *-gòmbè ŋóombe; plaie *-dòndà cidóonda – schèmes HB: rêve *-dóótò ndóoto; chanson *-yímbò ɲíimbo – schèmes BH: plume *-yòyá izoóya; maison *-yùmbá ɲuúmba – schèmes HH: corne *-pémbé ihéembe; cou *-kị́ŋgó síiŋgo [fn. 1] En gogo, tous les thèmes de forme -cvncv ont une voyelle longue. [Annexe, p. 509] Gogo: 1.: oui (réalisée seulement sur pénultième ou anté-pénultième) (2) 3.: langue accentuelle à mélodie H* 4.: 2 5.: H sur la pénultième ou sur l'antépénultième 6.: absente (7) 8.: syllabe finale extra-métrique; marque finale se rétracte sur une pénultième longue; H à la syllabe marquée 9.: ? 10.: cf. 8

sweep_summary: Gogo (gogo1263) is not in the catalog. it was copied into the gogo1263 folder, read in full for Gogo, and page scan 417, 418, 496, 509 were checked to verify the tone marks. Philippson treats Gogo (G11, group XVII Seuta-Ruvu) from his own field notes plus Rossel 1988: it is a 'langue accentuelle à mélodie H*' in which every short-vowel disyllabic stem carries the H accent on the antepenultimate syllable (falling tone on the penult in disyllabic words), only long-penult *BH stems keep a penultimate accent, final H is limited to some verb tenses, the final syllable is extrametrical, and vowel length surfaces only on the penult/antepenult (pp. 417-419, 484, 496, annex p. 509). Gogo is not among his languages with a demarcative length/pitch culmination on the penult (p. 483). Relevance: word-stress-of-this-language (accent placement), bearing: no-catalog-record. Beyond the item list: Großerhode 1998 'Ton und Druck im Gogo' (Diss. Bayreuth, VIII+176 pp; DNB idn 961115785) is the most relevant unread source (print only; DNB OPAC and Bayreuth ePub gave no online copy; Suleiman 2018 p. 8 reports it second-hand as finding Mpwapwa Gogo 'developing stress system to replace the tones') — high priority to acquire; Nurse & Mazengo 1979 'Gogo' (African Languages 5(1): 70-76, 101-104) could not be reached (Google Books search-inside bot-walled by automated download, API 429). HathiTrust (not reachable by automated download), Glottolog langdoc and archive.org searches yielded nothing further.

new_statements.quote: Vowels can bear tones – high and low. […] Rugemalira and Muzale (2014) points out that the tonal patterns across dialects of Gogo vary significantly and are the main difference between them. This statement can be backed by the fact discovered by Grosserhode and published in his monograph (Grosserhode, 1998). While analyzing the Mpwapwa dialect he came to the conclusion that Gogo language is experiencing changes in its tonal system. The language is developing stress system to replace the tones and this process is going on with different speed and in different directions in different dialects.

new_statements.rule_in_words: Gogo is a tone language (lexical H/L on vowels, grammatical tone in verbs); according to Großerhode 1998 as reported by Suleiman, a stress system is emerging that replaces tone, at different rates in different dialects. Where that stress falls is NOT stated in any source opened.
new_statements.exceptions: Dialects differ: the tone-to-stress shift is said to proceed 'with different speed and in different directions in different dialects'; tonal patterns are the main inter-dialect difference (Rugemalira & Muzale 2014 as cited).
new_statements.domain_note: Word-level lexical tone (minimal pair kufú:ta vs kufû:ta) and grammatical tone in the verb; the stress remark concerns the language system as a whole (Mpwapwa dialect per Großerhode), not citation forms or phrase level. No domain for a stress rule is given because no placement rule is given.
new_statements.first_reading: tone language with a stress statement
new_statements.identity_note: The second-hand stress remark concerns the Mpwapwa dialect (eastern Gogo area, i.e. the Tumba/Citumba 'East Gogo' zone in Wikipedia's dialect list) as analysed by Großerhode 1998; the tone data quoted from Kiruya 2012 concern Cinyambwa (West Gogo). Glottolog 5.1 lists no dialect glottocodes under gogo1263, so both fall under gogo1263. Suleiman 2018 (citing Mnyampala 1954) names five dialects: Cinyambwa, Cinya-Ugogo (central), Cinamaseya (north), Cinya-Takama (south), Kozisamba (interior south).

Exemples : [BB] dent *-gègò íjego, jambe *-gùdù múgulu; [HB] huile *-kútà máfuta, pluie *-búdà mvûla; [BH] canne à sucre *-gùbá íguva, oiseau *-dègé ndêje; [HH] graine *-béyú mbêyu, poulet *-kúkú ŋkûku. ³ Quand le mot est dissyllabique, l'accent antépénultième se réalise comme un ton tombant. (p. 417) — En revanche, les thèmes *-cv̀v̀cv́ manifestent encore une opposition : ils sont les seuls à avoir donné, en gogo, un accent sur la pénultième (p. 418)
new_statements.translation: In Gogo the oppositions have been reduced even further, since the *-cvcv stems have been brought down entirely to a single realisation, namely: accent on the antepenultimate. Examples: [BB] tooth *-gègò íjego, leg *-gùdù múgulu; [HB] oil *-kútà máfuta, rain *-búdà mvûla; [BH] sugar-cane *-gùbá íguva, bird *-dègé ndêje; [HH] seed *-béyú mbêyu, chicken *-kúkú ŋkûku. Fn. 3: When the word is disyllabic, the antepenultimate accent is realised as a falling tone. (p. 417) — On the other hand the *-cv̀v̀cv́ stems still show an opposition: they are the only ones to have yielded, in Gogo, an accent on the penultimate (p. 418). [Annex p. 509: 'Gogo: accentual language with H* melody; 2 schemes; H on the penultimate or on the antepenultimate; final syllable extrametrical; a final mark retracts onto a long penultimate; H on the marked syllable.']

new_statements.reading: First-hand (author's own field notes plus Rossel 1988) description: Gogo is a restricted pitch accent language ('langue accentuelle à mélodie H*'), not a stress language with a fixed demarcative position. The culminative H accent falls on the antepenultimate syllable of the word for all short-vowel disyllabic stems (surfacing as a falling tone on the penult of disyllabic words), and on the penultimate only for stems with a long penult that reflect Common Bantu *BH; final-syllable H is confined to certain verb tenses; the final syllable is extrametrical and vowel length surfaces only on the penult/antepenult. Philippson does not list Gogo among the East Bantu languages with a length or pitch culmination on the penultimate (p. 483). A catalog record would therefore have to code Gogo as tonal/pitch accent with antepenultimate (default) vs penultimate (long-penult) H placement, not as penultimate stress; a metrical reading is possible (extrametrical final + accent on the preceding syllable) but is Philippson's inference, not a stress claim.

sources.note: Gogo is classed as a 'langue accentuelle à mélodie H*' — a culminative pitch accent system, not a stress language. All bimoraic (-cvcv) noun stems have collapsed to a single pattern with the accent (H) on the antepenultimate syllable of the word (realised as a falling tone on the penult when the word is disyllabic: mvûla, ndêje, ŋkûku); only stems with a long penult reflecting Common Bantu *BH keep an accent on the penultimate (ɲuúmba, izoóya); a H on the final occurs only in certain verb tenses (p. 419).
